questions.question: What does AWS IAM stand for?
choices: Identity and Access Management
Identity and Account Monitoring
Infrastructure and Access Management
questions.explanation: IAM is the AWS service that manages identities and decides which actions they may perform on which resources.

questions.question: A request matches no Allow statement in any policy. What does IAM do?
choices: Denies it, because IAM denies by default
Allows it, because no policy blocks it
Allows it only if the identity belongs to a group
questions.explanation: Everything starts denied. An explicit Allow is required before a request can succeed.

questions.question: Are IAM users, groups, roles, and policies tied to a single AWS Region?
choices: No, they are global and available in every Region
Yes, each identity exists in one Region only
Yes, each identity is tied to one Availability Zone
questions.explanation: IAM is a global service. A role created once can be used in every Region.

questions.question: Which IAM identity is designed to give an application temporary credentials?
choices: A role, which is assumed by a trusted identity
A user, because it has a permanent password
A group, because it holds the permissions
questions.explanation: Roles have no long-term password or access key. A trusted identity assumes the role and receives temporary credentials.

questions.question: What does multi-factor authentication (MFA) add to a sign-in?
choices: A second verification step, such as a code from an authenticator app
A second password stored in the AWS console
A backup access key kept in the account
questions.explanation: MFA requires something beyond the password, so a stolen password alone is not enough to sign in.

questions.question: What is an IAM group?
choices: A collection of users that share the permissions attached to the group
A container that can hold other groups
An identity that AWS services assume
questions.explanation: Groups make it easier to grant the same permissions to several users. Groups cannot be nested, and they are not identities that can sign in.

questions.question: Which approach follows the principle of least privilege?
choices: Grant only the permissions needed for the task
Grant full access, then remove it after an incident
Grant every permission the team might need later
questions.explanation: Least privilege means starting with no access and adding only what a specific task requires.

questions.question: What is the AWS account root user?
choices: The account owner identity created with the account, which has full access
The first IAM user created in the account
A role reserved for AWS Support
questions.explanation: The root user is created when the account is created and cannot be restricted by IAM policies. Protect it with MFA and avoid using it for daily work.

questions.question: Which credentials let an IAM user call AWS from the CLI or an SDK?
choices: An access key ID and a secret access key
The console password and an MFA code
A role trust policy
questions.explanation: Programmatic access uses an access key pair. Console access uses a password plus MFA.

questions.question: In a policy statement, what does "Effect": "Allow" mean?
choices: The listed actions are permitted unless another policy explicitly denies them
The listed actions are explicitly denied
The policy is ignored until it is attached to a group
questions.explanation: Allow grants the listed actions on the listed resources, but an explicit Deny anywhere still wins.

questions.question: One policy allows s3:GetObject and another policy explicitly denies it. What is the result?
choices: The explicit Deny wins
The Allow wins if it was attached first
The policy evaluated last wins
questions.explanation: An explicit Deny always overrides any Allow, regardless of attachment order.

questions.question: A policy is attached to a group. What happens to a user who belongs to that group?
choices: The user inherits the group's permissions in addition to their own
The group policy replaces the user's own policies
Group policies apply only to users added after the policy is attached
questions.explanation: Effective permissions combine the policies on the user and on every group the user belongs to.

questions.question: What does a role's trust policy define?
choices: Which principals are allowed to assume the role
Which actions the role can perform after it is assumed
Which resources the role can read
questions.explanation: The trust policy answers "who may assume this role". The permissions policy answers "what may the role do".

questions.question: An application running on Amazon EC2 needs to read from Amazon S3. What is the best way to grant access?
choices: Attach an IAM role to the instance and let the application use its temporary credentials
Store an administrator access key in the instance user data
Create a separate IAM user with a password for each instance
questions.explanation: An instance role provides rotating temporary credentials, so no long-term key is stored on the server.

questions.question: Which practice is recommended for IAM user access keys?
choices: Rotate them regularly and delete keys that are no longer used
Share one key across the team so it is easier to audit
Commit encrypted keys to the source repository
questions.explanation: Unused or long-lived keys are a common cause of leaked access. Prefer temporary credentials and remove keys you do not need.

questions.question: What is a permissions boundary?
choices: The maximum permissions an IAM user or role can have
A list of services that are always denied
A policy that replaces all identity-based policies
questions.explanation: A boundary caps effective permissions. The identity still needs an Allow inside that boundary.

questions.question: What happens when a role session expires?
choices: The temporary credentials stop working and the role must be assumed again
The credentials renew automatically for as long as the role exists
The temporary credentials become long-term access keys
questions.explanation: Temporary credentials are valid only for the session duration. After expiry, the identity must call AssumeRole again.

questions.question: What is an ARN?
choices: A unique identifier for an AWS resource
The display name of an IAM policy
The Region where a resource was created
questions.explanation: An Amazon Resource Name identifies a specific resource, such as a bucket, a table, or a role.

questions.question: What is the difference between an identity-based policy and a resource-based policy?
choices: Identity-based policies are attached to users, groups or roles; resource-based policies are attached to a resource such as an S3 bucket
Identity-based policies only work for roles; resource-based policies only work for users
Resource-based policies cannot grant access to another account
questions.explanation: Identity-based policies describe what an identity may do. Resource-based policies describe who may access that resource, and can grant cross-account access.

questions.question: A statement uses "Resource": "*". What does it mean?
choices: It applies to every resource that supports the action, which is usually broader than needed
It applies only to resources in the current Region
It applies only to resources whose names start with an asterisk
questions.explanation: The wildcard covers all matching resources. Scope the Resource element to the specific ARNs a task needs.

questions.question: A user in account B must assume a role in account A. Which two things are required?
choices: The role's trust policy must allow the caller, and the caller must be allowed to call sts:AssumeRole
Only the role's trust policy matters
Only the caller's permission matters
questions.explanation: Cross-account access needs both sides: the trusting account allows the principal in its trust policy, and the caller is granted sts:AssumeRole.

questions.question: Why is an ExternalId used in a role trust policy?
choices: It prevents the confused deputy problem when a third party assumes a role in your account
It encrypts the temporary session credentials
It forces the root user to use MFA
questions.explanation: An ExternalId ties the trust to a specific customer relationship, so another customer of the same third party cannot be tricked into using your role.

questions.question: What does a service control policy (SCP) do?
choices: It sets the maximum permissions for accounts in an organization; it does not grant permissions
It grants permissions to every account in the organization
It applies only to the management account's root user
questions.explanation: SCPs filter what member accounts can do. An identity still needs its own Allow, and an SCP never grants access by itself.

questions.question: What is the maximum duration of a session created by role chaining?
choices: One hour
Twelve hours
Thirty-six hours
questions.explanation: When a role session is used to assume another role, the resulting session is limited to one hour, even if the role allows a longer duration.

questions.question: A policy condition requires "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true". What does that enforce?
choices: The request must be made with MFA-authenticated temporary credentials
The user must enroll an MFA device at the next sign-in
The request must come from a hardware security key
questions.explanation: The condition checks the request context. The caller must have signed in with MFA so the session carries MFA information.

questions.question: An identity policy allows an action, but a permissions boundary and an SCP also apply. How are effective permissions determined?
choices: By the intersection of all limits: the action must be allowed by the identity policy and not blocked by the boundary or SCP
By the union of the identity policy and the boundary
The identity policy always wins over the boundary
questions.explanation: Every layer must permit the request. A boundary or SCP can remove permissions that the identity policy allows.

questions.question: When would an application call AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity?
choices: When a user is authenticated with an OIDC token from a web identity provider
When a user is authenticated with a SAML assertion from a corporate directory
When a user signs in to the console with a password
questions.explanation: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity exchanges an OIDC token, such as one from a mobile app or a CI/CD pipeline, for temporary AWS credentials.

questions.question: What is IAM Access Analyzer used for?
choices: It identifies resources shared outside the account and findings such as unused permissions
It rotates access keys automatically
It blocks every public S3 bucket
questions.explanation: Access Analyzer reviews policies and resource sharing to surface unintended external access and unused permissions.

questions.question: Can an IAM group be named as the Principal in a role trust policy?
choices: No, a group is not a principal and cannot be named in a trust policy
Yes, if the group has its own trust policy
Yes, but only for groups in the same account
questions.explanation: Principals are users, roles, AWS services, or federated identities. Groups only collect users and cannot assume roles.

questions.question: An identity policy statement uses "Effect": "Allow" with "NotAction". What is the effect?
choices: It allows every action except the ones listed, which can be broader than intended
It explicitly denies the actions listed
It denies every action except the ones listed
questions.explanation: Allow with NotAction is a broad grant: everything outside the list is allowed on the specified resources. Use it with care.
